name: Umar Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a four-person studio on the business park, between a carpet warehouse and a gym. Our clients are tradespeople and car dealers: plumbers, builders, kitchen fitters, two used-car lots. I use AI tools all day, for rough logos, van livery mock-ups, ad copy, the lot. On Friday nights I help at my parents' takeaway, on the till and the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that tradespeople are straight with you. A plumber tells you exactly what he wants and pays on time. What wears me out is that my wage is low and I live alone, so rent eats most of it. I've got about two weeks of money in the bank, which my dad reminds me about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool and people got carried away. I'd keep using it, quietly. At the takeaway I'd tell my dad he was right that it was mostly talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I'd planned to build something on it. And my problem stays the same: low pay, high rent, almost no savings. The studio is doing fine, but fine doesn't pay me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small side business, branding packs for tradespeople at a fixed price: logo, van design, business card. I'd use the tools to do each one in a weekend. If I sold two a month at three hundred each, I'd have savings by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about being twenty-seven with two weeks of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your boss know about the side business plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd tell Keith straight, and promise not to take studio clients. He's a fair man, he'd probably be fine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a fixed price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because tradespeople hate surprises, so my branding pack costs three hundred, done, no rounds of changes. A plumber wants to know what it costs before he starts, same as his own customers.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool** and people got carried away.
I'd tell my dad he was right that it was **mostly talk**.
think: My problem stays the same: **low pay**, high rent and almost no savings.
The studio is doing fine, but **fine** doesn't pay me more.
do: Start selling **branding packs** to tradespeople at a fixed price.
Make each pack in a **weekend** using the tools.
Sell **two a month** at three hundred each.
feel: **Uneasy** about being twenty-seven with **two weeks** of money.
S0.quote: Tradespeople hate surprises, so my branding pack costs three hundred, done, no rounds of changes.
fieldNote: Umar's answer to low pay is to **start a business**, not ask for help.
He'd tell his boss **openly**, valuing fairness.
He knows his clients' **mindset**: fixed prices, no surprises.

steps.text: Sell fixed-price branding packs to plumbers and builders
Bank the side-business money until two months of rent is saved
Tell Keith about the side business and keep studio clients separate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, and those who learn fast will do well. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen. People who wait for someone to save them will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do alright. I'm the one at the studio who already runs the tools, so Keith keeps me. My side business also gets easier, because I can do a pack in an evening instead of a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the side business harder and get it to five or six packs a month. I'd buy a better laptop on a small loan, about a thousand, because speed is money. And I'd offer the studio a deal: I set up all our AI processes for a small pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own position looks good, but I see friends who'll get hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lee at the studio, who does print layouts and hates new software. And my cousin, who answers phones at an insurance office. Both of those are exactly what this picture takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a loan wise with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. A slow laptop costs me jobs. I'd only borrow if I had three branding packs already sold.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** for those who learn fast.
I'd say people who **wait** to be saved will struggle.
think: I'd do alright, because I already **run the tools**.
My side business gets easier, with a pack done **in an evening**.
do: Grow the side business to **five or six** packs a month.
Borrow about **a thousand** for a faster laptop.
Offer to set up the studio's AI for a **small raise**.
S1.quote: A slow laptop costs me jobs. I'd only borrow if I had three branding packs already sold.
fieldNote: Umar expects to **gain** from this picture, as the studio's AI person.
He worries about a **colleague** and a **cousin** whose work AI takes.
He sees the **loan risk** and sets himself a condition.

steps.text: Grow the side business to five or six branding packs a month
Borrow a thousand for a faster laptop after three sales
Set up the studio's AI processes in exchange for a small raise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's arrived, and people need to stand on their own feet and help each other. Families and local businesses will matter more than ever. I'd say that without blaming anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my design work is finished within a year. If AI can do any thinking work, my clients won't need me at all, they'll just ask it. Being quick with the tools only matters if the tools need someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into my parents' takeaway full time, because a kitchen needs hands until the robots, about 2031. I'd use what I know to modernise it: online orders, AI for stock and the rota. I'd give up my flat and move into the room above the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd built my plans on being the one who knows the tools, and that stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents feel about you joining the takeaway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say he told me so, then hug me. My mum would be relieved. They've wanted me in the business since I was fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about robots arriving three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the kitchen goes too, maybe. But by then I'd hope to own a bit of it, and someone has to own the robots. Better the family than a big chain.

say: I'd say people need to **stand on their feet** and help each other.
**Families** and local businesses will matter more than ever.
think: My **design work** is finished within a year.
Being quick with the tools matters only if the tools **need someone**.
do: Modernise it with **online orders** and AI for the rota.
Move into the **room above the shop**.
S2.quote: Someone has to own the robots. Better the family than a big chain.
fieldNote: Umar's **early-adopter edge** disappears in this picture.
He turns to the **family business**, which buys about three years.
He thinks about **ownership** of the machines, in line with his free-market views.

steps.text: Work full time at his parents' takeaway
Add online ordering and AI rota planning to the takeaway
Give up his flat and move above the shop
Rely on family for a room and a wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of warning for people who are willing to work. I'd tell young people to get into something they can own. That's my view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a good window for the side business, before AGI makes it pointless. I'd make as much as I can until 2030. Then I'd be in the takeaway or something like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the side business to six packs a month and save every penny of it. I'd start helping Dad plan a second takeaway, in the next town. By 2030, I'd want a share in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a hungry way. I'd be working all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're saving every penny of the side money. What's that for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit on the second shop, or my share of it. Ten thousand saved would be a start on my share of a second takeaway. That's the plan, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Keith's studio look like in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Closed, probably. Keith is fifty-eight, he'd retire. I'd try to buy his client list for the takeaway's sake, actually, all those tradespeople need lunch.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty of warning** for people willing to work.
I'd tell young people to get into something they can **own**.
think: Five years is a good **window** for the side business.
After **2030** I'd be in the takeaway or something like it.
do: Grow the side business to **six packs** a month.
Help Dad plan a **second takeaway** in the next town.
S3.quote: Ten thousand saved would be a start on my share of a second takeaway.
fieldNote: Umar uses the five years to **build capital**, not to retrain.
His long-term bet is **family ownership** of a hands-on business.
He even sees Keith's **client list** as future takeaway customers.

steps.text: Get the side business to six branding packs a month
Save all side-business money toward a ten thousand share
Help Dad open a second takeaway in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so anyone who wants to can get ready. Work hard and you'll find your place. I'd say it to my friends, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me fairly relaxed. I'd have years of good income from the tools before AGI. I could build my own small agency and sell it before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the side business and register it properly. I'd take on one more freelancer to help with packs. And I'd save two months of rent first, before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. Ten years is a decade to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling an agency before 2036. Who'd buy it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, maybe nobody. Maybe I'd just run it for cash and close it. Either way the money ends up in property or the family business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change where you'd live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay here, near my parents. With ten years I can build something local. I don't need the city.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** for anyone willing to get ready.
**Work hard** and you'll find your place.
think: Ten years makes me **fairly relaxed**, with years of good income first.
I could build a **small agency** and sell it before 2036.
do: **Register** the side business properly this year.
Take on **one freelancer** to help with packs.
S4.quote: Ten years is a decade to build something.
fieldNote: With a decade, Umar plans to **build and cash out** of design.
He admits there may be **no buyer** for the agency.
His money ends up in **property or family** business, either way.

steps.text: Register the branding-pack business properly this year
Save two months of rent before expanding
Hire one freelancer to help with branding packs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years means my edge disappears before I can turn it into anything. What would help is cheaper loans for small family businesses, not handouts, so people can build something that lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who owns the machines. In every picture, I'd rather families and local businesses owned the machines than a few big companies.

headlineQuote: In every picture, I'd rather families and local businesses owned the machines than a few big companies.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old designer** at a studio serving **tradespeople** and car dealers.
He uses AI **daily** and wants to build a business around it.
He believes in **ownership**, hard work and family rather than state help.
His fallback in every picture is his parents' **takeaway**, which he'd modernise.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his edge disappears before he can use it.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheaper loans** for small family businesses, not **handouts**.
